title: E. coli Meningitis Presenting in a Patient with Disseminated Strongyloides stercoralis
case_prompt: A 43-year-old Hispanic man from Peru with remote travel in the Peruvian and Brazilian jungles two decades prior was diagnosed with Bell’s palsy three weeks earlier and started on prednisone 50 mg twice daily without follow-up. He presented with a three-week history of diarrhea, a 10-kg weight loss, intermittent fevers, and three days of hematochezia. On examination he was pale and tachycardic, had mild abdominal tenderness, and blood on rectal examination; the remainder of the physical exam was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 16 000 cells/mm^3 (82% neutrophils, 2% eosinophils, 7% bands), hemoglobin 8 g/dL, and platelets 700 000/mm^3. He was presumed to have diverticulitis and was started on intravenous ciprofloxacin and metronidazole. One week after admission, he became drowsy with bradylalia and bradypsychia, developed nuchal rigidity with positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs, fever, right lower‐lobe crackles, abdominal distension, and constipation. A lumbar puncture yielded cloudy fluid with a protein of 179 mg/dL, glucose of 5 mg/dL, 2070 leukocytes/mm^3 (92% neutrophils), and Gram‐negative rods on Gram stain. Repeat blood count showed 25 000 leukocytes/mm^3 (84% neutrophils, 0% eosinophils, 7% bands). A CT scan of the abdomen revealed a dilated ascending colon.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Diverticulitis was initially suspected based on abdominal pain, diarrhea, hematochezia, and leukocytosis — “The patient was suspected to have diverticulitis.”  
2. Ulcerative colitis was considered after pancolitis was seen on colonoscopy — “Results indicated pancolitis and suggested to rule out ulcerative colitis…”  
3. Parasitic colitis entered the differential given gastrointestinal symptoms and pancolitis — “Results indicated … and suggested to rule out … parasitosis.”  
4. Intestinal tuberculosis was also considered in the face of chronic diarrhea and colonic inflammation — “Results indicated … and suggested to rule out … tuberculosis.”  
5. Hospital-acquired ESBL-producing Escherichia coli meningitis was deemed likely because the meningitis developed after several days in hospital — “the extended spectrum β-lactamase producing Escherichia coli causing our patient's meningitis was most likely hospital-acquired since he developed the infection after being hospitalized for several days.”  
6. HIV infection was excluded as a predisposing factor by a negative ELISA test — “An ELISA test for HIV was performed with a negative result.”  
7. Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome was identified as the unifying diagnosis because corticosteroid use in an asymptomatic carrier can trigger disseminated infection with bacterial translocation — “The autoinfection cycle of SS allows it to cause both parasitic and enteric bacterial infections at distant locations in the body…”
